records.rationale: Correct extension of the determinant of a square matrix to commutative rings, including polynomial entries. The algebraic formula uses addition, additive inverses and multiplication, with no division requirement.

records.rationale: The negative- and positive-real-part criteria are correct for the stated constant-coefficient linear ODE. However, the blanket claim that eigenvalues determine stability needs qualification on the imaginary axis: Jordan block sizes also matter. The answer does not distinguish that case from a simple oscillatory mode.

evidence.title: MIT OpenCourseWare, Eigenvalues and Stability
evidence.finding: For a continuous-time constant-coefficient linear differential equation, asymptotic stability is governed by negative real parts of eigenvalues, rather than their maximum modulus.

evidence.title: James Demmel, Berkeley MA221 Lecture 15
evidence.finding: Defines eigenvalues through the characteristic determinant and nonzero null vectors; shows similarity preserves eigenvalues and presents unique Jordan blocks up to ordering.

The real matrix [[0,-1,1,0],[1,0,0,1],[0,0,0,-1],[0,0,1,0]] has characteristic polynomial (lambda^2+1)^2 and solution (t*cos(t),t*sin(t),cos(t),sin(t)), whose squared norm is t^2+1. The same eigenvalue multiset with diagonalizable rotation blocks has bounded solutions; eigenvalues alone do not settle marginal stability.

records.rationale: The direction-dependent limiting behavior is useful, but denominator zeros are described too uniformly as curves analogous to vertical asymptotes. A nonzero real bivariate polynomial can have isolated real zeros, and bounded rational behavior or cancellation can occur instead of divergence.

evidence.finding: For coprime real polynomials, a real denominator root a has P(a) nonzero by the factor theorem. Writing Q(x)=(x-a)^k R(x) with R(a) nonzero gives a pole.

Q=x^2+y^2 has a real zero set consisting only of (0,0). The coprime rational function x^2/(x^2+y^2) stays between 0 and 1 near its excluded origin. The unreduced expression (x+y)/(x+y) also equals 1 off its excluded line, so the zero locus alone does not establish asymptotic blow-up.

records.rationale: Valid group-theoretic proof of Euler's theorem using the unit group modulo n, its totient order and Lagrange's theorem.

evidence.finding: For positive modulus n, invertible residue classes form a group of size phi(n). Lagrange gives ord([a]) dividing phi(n), so [a]^phi(n)=[1].
For a residue class a with gcd(a,n)=1, its finite order d divides phi(n); writing phi(n)=kd gives [a]^phi(n)=([a]^d)^k=[1].
The standard theorem assumes an integer a and positive integer modulus n; the proof uses those conventional modular-arithmetic domains.
